title: Caste, honestly
hook: the Gurus rejected caste, yet caste divisions still show in some Sikh places

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan, and your line was a conversation open. Did you listen to the side you usually skip? Today, a harder conversation, told honestly. Day one thousand thirty-six.

In the langar hall, everyone sits on the floor in the same row. The farmer next to the doctor, the cleaner next to the landlord, all eating the same food from the same kitchen. That row is a sermon without words. Now drive out to some villages in Punjab, and you may find two gurdwaras within walking distance of each other. Same Guru, same hymns. Different families, divided by caste. A row on the floor says one thing. Two buildings say another. Today is about the gap between them.
screen: `ONE ROW ON THE FLOOR.` → `TWO GURDWARAS, ONE VILLAGE.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: First, what the Gurus said. At Ang 349 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says to recognize the divine light in everyone and not to ask about caste, because in the world beyond there is no caste. At Ang 15 he says he stands with the lowest of the low, and has nothing to do with the great. Guru Amar Das, in a hymn at Ang 1127, warns: let no one be proud of caste. The Guru Granth Sahib itself holds hymns by bhagats from castes that others looked down on, set beside the Gurus' own words. Second, what the Gurus did. Langar, where all sit in one row. The sangat, where all sit on one floor. And the Khalsa, where, tradition says, those who first came forward were from different castes and drank amrit from one bowl. Third, the honest part. Caste did not disappear. In some places it still shows: in separate gurdwaras, in marriages arranged within a caste, in surnames that carry old ranks, and in Sikhs from castes once called low who say they are still made to feel it. Sikh writers, reformers and Dalit Sikhs themselves have called this out, using the Gurus' own words. Fourth, the line. A path is not judged only by how well its followers keep it. It also gives them a standard to be measured by. On caste, the standard is not in doubt. That is today's line: the gurus rejected it. The work is in the gap between the hymn and the village.
screen: `ANG 349: DON'T ASK ABOUT CASTE.` · `ONE ROW, ONE FLOOR, ONE BOWL.` · `CASTE STILL SHOWS IN SOME PLACES.` · `THE STANDARD IS NOT IN DOUBT.` · then, large: `THE GURUS REJECTED IT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with one bias. Sit, and let your breath slow. People get sorted in many ways: by accent, by job, by neighborhood, by family name, by school. Gently ask yourself whether you sort anyone without meaning to. Don't punish yourself for it. If one comes, just look at it. Breathe in, and look at it plainly. Breathe out, and picture the langar row: you sitting next to exactly the person that bias would put somewhere else. Stay in that row a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Caste. An old ranking of people by birth that the Gurus rejected in word and practice, and that still shows in some Sikh places. Today's word.

Your line: the gurus rejected it. This week crossed borders: Pakistan, gurdwara, pardes, North America, then rights, women's voices and caste. Today, catch one bias of your own in the act, and sit in the row anyway. Day one thousand thirty-six.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, all eat together in langar sitting in one row, and the Rehat Maryada rejects caste distinctions; in some places caste still shapes marriages and gurdwara membership, and Sikh reformers work against it.

what a scholar hears: the Guru Granth Sahib's critique of caste is explicit and repeated, and the gap between that standard and village practice is itself an old theme of Sikh reform.
